# Heat-related illnesses

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Neurology > Disorders of consciousness > Heat-related illnesses*

[Original Article Link](/library/yL0dZS)

---

## Summary

Heat-related illnesses are pathological conditions caused by <u>hyperthermia</u>, an elevated body temperature caused by an impaired ability to maintain temperature at the normal <u>hypothalamic</u> set point. Underlying <u>causes of hyperthermia</u> include <u>endogenous</u>, environmental, and behavioral factors which can be present concurrently, increasing the risk of heat-related illnesses. Minor heat-related illnesses include heat <u>syncope</u>, <u>heat rash</u>, heat <u>edema</u>, and heat cramps. <u>Heat exhaustion</u>, a moderate heat-related illness, is characterized by <u>dehydration</u>, normal or slightly elevated body temperature (typically â¤ 40.0Â°C), and normal mental status. Clinical features include symptoms of <u>dehydration</u>, <u>nausea</u>, <u>headache</u>, <u>weakness</u>, and <u>ataxia</u>. <u>Heat exhaustion</u> is typically treated with rehydration, <u>passive cooling</u>, and, if needed, <u>evaporative and convective cooling</u> (e.g., mist and fan). Aggressive <u>active cooling</u> is usually unnecessary and complications are uncommon. <u>Heatstroke</u> is a life-threatening heat-related illness characterized by severe <u>hyperthermia</u> (with a body temperature typically > 40.0Â°C) and severe <u>CNS</u> dysfunction. The cornerstone of treatment is aggressive <u>active cooling</u> to reduce core body temperature to less than 40.0Â°C. Methods include <u>conductive cooling</u> (e.g., ice water immersion) or <u>evaporative and convective cooling</u> combined with adjunct cooling measures (e.g., cooled <u>IV fluids</u> or ice packs). Management of complications (e.g., <u>acute kidney injury</u> and <u>rhabdomyolysis</u>) and <u>ICU</u> admission are often required.

---

## Overview

### Hyperthermia




* Elevated body temperature caused by an inability to maintain temperature at the normal <u>hypothalamic</u> setpoint, i.e., <u>thermoregulatory</u> dysfunction or failure

* Causes include <u>endogenous</u>, environmental, and behavioral factors and many disease states (see “<u>Causes of hyperthermia</u>”).

* Can be a manifestation of an underlying disease or the cause of a heat-related illness

* Treated primarily with cooling (see “<u>Management of hyperthermia</u>”)





> [!TIP]
> Elevated body temperature alone is insufficient to diagnose <u>hyperthermia</u> or heat-related illness in athletes, as it is a common physiological response to strenuous exertion. [[1]](/library/SMWyLN0)[[2]](/library/gMWFLN0)




### Overview of heat-related illnesses




Heat-related illnesses are pathological conditions caused by <u>hyperthermia</u>.




| <br>Overview of heat-related illnesses [[2]](/library/gMWFLN0)[[3]](/library/B5WzmN0)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Minor heat-related illnesses | <u>Heat exhaustion</u> | <u>Heatstroke</u> |
| Description | <br><br>* Heat <u>syncope</u><br><br>* Heat <u>edema</u><br><br>* Heat cramps<br><br>* <u>Heat rash</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Mild to moderate heat-related illness<br><br>* Variable <u>nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>, <u>diaphoresis</u>, <u>tachycardia</u>, and/or <u>dehydration</u><br><br>* Normal mental status<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Life-threatening heat-related illness<br><br>* Variable <u>nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>, <u>tachypnea</u>, <u>tachycardia</u>, and/or <u>hypotension</u><br><br>* Variable changes in <u>skin</u> moisture and muscle tone<br><br>* Severe <u>CNS</u> dysfunction<br><br><br> |
| Body temperature | <br>* Often minimally elevated<br><br> | <br>* Mild to moderate elevation; typically â¤ 40Â°C (â¤ 104Â°F)<br><br> | <br>* Severe elevation; typically > 40Â°C (> 104Â°F)<br><br> |
| Underlying etiology | <br><br>* Typically caused by high ambient temperature<br><br>* Heat cramps are commonly associated with exercise and internal heat generation.<br><br><br> | <br>* Typically high ambient temperature with or without other <u>causes of hyperthermia</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Underlying <u>causes of hyperthermia</u> vary.<br><br>* <u>Exertional heatstroke</u>: usually strenuous exertion combined with high ambient temperature<br><br>* <u>Nonexertional heatstroke</u>: usually high ambient temperature<br><br><br> |
| Management | <br><br>* <u>Supportive care</u><br><br>* See “<u>Syncope</u>.”<br><br>* See “<u>Miliaria</u>.”<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Passive cooling</u><br><br>* Oral rehydration<br><br>* <u>Active cooling</u> in severe cases<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Immediate <u>active cooling</u><br><br>* Aggressive <u>supportive care</u><br><br>* Treatment of complications<br><br>* Possible <u>ICU</u> admission<br><br><br> |





> [!WARNING]
> Heat-related illnesses exist on a spectrum, and manifestations of <u>heat exhaustion</u> and <u>heatstroke</u> can overlap. When in doubt, treat any heat-related illness with severe features as <u>heatstroke</u>.

---

## Etiology

### Causes of hyperthermia [[3]](/library/B5WzmN0)[[4]](/library/kIYm1q)[[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




Multiple concurrent <u>risk factors</u> for <u>hyperthermia</u> increase the likelihood of developing a heat-related illness.




#### Increased <u>heat production</u>




* Behavioral factors

* Strenuous exercise

* <u>Stimulant intoxication</u>

* Conditions

* <u>Sepsis</u>

* <u>Status epilepticus</u>

* <u>Thyroid storm</u>

* <u>Neuroleptic malignant syndrome</u>

* <u>Malignant hyperthermia</u>

* <u>Serotonin syndrome</u>





#### Decreased heat dissipation




* Environmental factors

* High ambient temperature and/or <u>humidity</u>

* Heavy clothing and/or equipment

* Conditions

* <u>Skin</u> disease, e.g., <u>erythroderma</u>, <u>anhidrosis</u>, <u>ichthyoses</u>, <u>scleroderma</u>

* <u>Burns</u>

* Reduced cutaneous <u>perfusion</u>, e.g., due to <u>heart failure</u>

* Substance-related factors

* Medications that impair thermoregulation, e.g., <u>anticholinergics</u>, <u>antihistamines</u>, <u>beta blockers</u>, <u>calcium channel blockers</u>

* <u>Alcohol</u> use





#### Limitations in adaptive behavior




Environmental, cognitive, and/or physical factors may limit appropriate responses to hot environments, e.g.:




* Inability to increase water intake

* Inability to remove oneself from the hot environment

* See “<u>Classification of heatstroke</u>” for detailed <u>risk factors</u>.

---

## Pathophysiology

* The normal physiological response to elevated body temperature includes: 

* <u>Hypothalamus</u>-mediated peripheral <u>vasodilation</u> (increased <u>heat convection</u> and radiation)

* Sweating (increased evaporation)

* In <u>hyperthermia</u>, the <u>hypothalamic</u> <u>thermoregulatory</u> response is inadequate to maintain a normal temperature.

* High body temperature → protein <u>denaturation</u>, phospholipid and <u>lipoprotein</u> damage, and membrane lipid <u>liquefaction</u> → cell damage and loss of function (including myocardiocytes and <u>neurons</u>) → cardiovascular collapse → <u>multi-organ failure</u> and possibly <u>death</u>

## Differential diagnoses

### <u>Hyperthermia</u> vs. <u>fever</u>




| <br><u>Hyperthermia</u> vs. <u>fever</u> [[3]](/library/B5WzmN0)[[4]](/library/kIYm1q)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | <u>Hyperthermia</u> | <u>Fever</u> |
| Mechanism | <br>* <u>Thermoregulatory</u> dysfunction, i.e., impaired ability to maintain normal function despite normal <u>hypothalamic</u> temperature set point<br><br> | <br>* Rise in <u>hypothalamic</u> temperature set point<br><br> |
| Causes | <br><br>* Increased <u>heat production</u><br><br>* Decreased heat dissipation<br><br>* Limitations in adaptive behavior<br><br>* See “<u>Causes of hyperthermia</u>” for details.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Infections<br><br>* Inflammatory disorders<br><br>* Medications<br><br>* See “<u>Fever</u>” for other causes.<br><br><br> |
| Management | <br><br>* Cooling (see “<u>Management of hyperthermia</u>” for details)<br><br>* Treatment of the underlying cause<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Antipyretics</u><br><br>* Treatment of the underlying cause<br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> <u>Sepsis</u> with <u>hyperpyrexia</u> can be mistaken for a heat-related illness. [[4]](/library/kIYm1q)




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

The following cooling methods can be used to treat all types of <u>hyperthermia</u>. The choice of a specific method depends on the <u>cause of hyperthermia</u>, local resources, and the patient's baseline condition. See “<u>Heat exhaustion</u>” and “<u>Heatstroke</u>” for specific treatment approaches.




### Approach [[1]](/library/SMWyLN0)[[2]](/library/gMWFLN0)[[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




Rapid reduction of core body temperature is critical to reducing mortality.




* Provide <u>advanced cardiac life support</u> and/or <u>airway management</u> if indicated.

* Begin <u>passive cooling</u>: Remove heat stressors, e.g., stop exercise, move to a cooler environment.

* Provide <u>fluid resuscitation</u> and <u>immediate hemodynamic support</u>.

* Initiate <u>active cooling</u> promptly for <u>heatstroke</u> and/or persistent <u>hyperthermia</u>.

* Continue <u>active cooling</u> until the core temperature is < 39Â°C (< 102Â°F).

* Consider adjunctive cooling measures (e.g., cold <u>IV fluids</u>) alongside other <u>active cooling</u> methods, if indicated.

* If <u>stimulant intoxication</u> is suspected, administer <u>benzodiazepines for stimulant intoxication</u>.





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Manage hyperthermia</u> with <u>active cooling</u> if there is any doubt about the severity of the illness.




### Passive cooling [[2]](/library/gMWFLN0)




* Definition: cooling methods that separate a patient from external heat sources and/or barriers to heat dissipation

* Indications

* Minor or moderate heat-related illness

* Severe heat-related illness only if <u>active cooling</u> is not immediately available

* Methods

* Move the patient to a cooler environment.

* Remove equipment and heavy clothing, e.g., helmet, pads, jersey, overalls.





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Passive cooling</u> is insufficient for treating <u>heatstroke</u>; initiate active cooling as soon as possible.




### Active cooling




* Definition: cooling methods that involve the application of a medium to facilitate <u>heat transfer</u> from the patient's body

* Methods

* <u>Conductive cooling</u> (most rapid and effective), e.g., ice water immersion, <u>skin</u> lavage or wrap

* <u>Evaporative and convective cooling</u> (usually most practical), e.g., mist and fan

* Adjunctive methods (limited use), e.g., cold <u>IV fluids</u>, ice packs, cooling blankets, internal lavage





#### Conductive cooling [[1]](/library/SMWyLN0)[[2]](/library/gMWFLN0)




* <u>Conductive cooling</u> involves direct <u>heat transfer</u> from the body to another material (typically water).

* It is the most effective method for rapid temperature reduction.  [[1]](/library/SMWyLN0)[[2]](/library/gMWFLN0)





> [!TIP]
> Immersion has the fastest cooling rate (∼ 0.2Â°C/min) compared to <u>skin</u> wrap and <u>evaporative and convective cooling</u> methods (0.1Â°C/min). [[1]](/library/SMWyLN0)[[2]](/library/gMWFLN0)[[3]](/library/B5WzmN0)




##### Immersion




* Indications

* Typically the first choice to treat severe <u>hyperthermia</u>

* Preferred method for <u>exertional heatstroke</u>; consider for <u>nonexertional heatstroke</u>.

* Technique: Place the patient in a tub of cold water (∼ 20Â°C) or ice water (∼ 2Â°C). [[1]](/library/SMWyLN0)





> [!WARNING]
> Immersion may interfere with other necessary lifesaving measures (e.g., <u>airway management</u>) in unstable patients with <u>heatstroke</u>.




##### <u>Skin</u> lavage or wrap




* Indications: alternative if immersion is unavailable, e.g., in the field

* Techniques

* Rotation of ice water-soaked towels or ice packs over the entire body

* Application of crushed ice slurry over a patient lying between plastic sheets [[2]](/library/gMWFLN0)





#### Evaporative and convective cooling [[2]](/library/gMWFLN0)[[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[6]](/library/B6WzMm0)




* <u>Evaporative cooling</u> involves the transfer of heat from the body to surrounding air and water molecules.

* Cooling is usually supported through convection, i.e., increasing the movement of air around the body.





> [!TIP]
> Although less effective than <u>conductive cooling</u>, <u>evaporative and convective cooling</u> methods are easier to implement and may be less stressful for frail patients. [[7]](/library/AeXRYx)




##### Indications




* Immersion unavailable

* <u>Frailty</u> and/or older age

* Simultaneous treatment of many patients, e.g., severe urban heat wave, marathon runners

* Associated conditions that make immersion difficult, e.g., <u>airway</u> compromise, active <u>vomiting</u>





##### “Mist and fan” technique




* Remove clothing.

* Spray or douse <u>skin</u> with cold water.

* Fan or blow air across wet <u>skin</u> to facilitate evaporation.





#### Adjunctive <u>active cooling</u> measures [[3]](/library/B5WzmN0)[[4]](/library/kIYm1q)[[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




Avoid the following as primary cooling methods; consider only in patients with severe <u>hyperthermia</u> if immersion is impractical or unavailable:




* Infusion of cold <u>IV fluids</u>

* Ice packs to the neck, groin, <u>axillae</u>

* <u>Bladder</u> and/or <u>gastric lavage</u> with cold fluids

* Commercial cooling blankets or vests

## Heat exhaustion

### Definition [[2]](/library/gMWFLN0)[[3]](/library/B5WzmN0)[[4]](/library/kIYm1q)




<u>Heat exhaustion</u> is a heat-related illness characterized by all of the following:




* Decrease in blood volume and/or <u>total body water</u> caused by <u>heat stress</u>

* Normal or slightly elevated core body temperature (typically defined as â¤ 40Â°C)

* Normal mental status  [[4]](/library/kIYm1q)[[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)





> [!TIP]
> In contrast with <u>heatstroke</u>, the <u>homeostatic</u> <u>thermoregulatory</u> system retains partial function, and heat continues to actively dissipate.




### Clinical features [[3]](/library/B5WzmN0)[[4]](/library/kIYm1q)[[8]](/library/x5WEmN0)




* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>

* <u>Diaphoresis</u>

* <u>Dehydration</u>, <u>tachycardia</u>, <u>orthostatic hypotension</u>

* <u>Headache</u>, <u>weakness</u>, fatigue

* <u>Dizziness</u>, <u>vertigo</u>, <u>ataxia</u>





### Diagnostics [[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* <u>Diagnostics for dehydration</u>: <u>BMP</u>, <u>CBC</u>, UA, urine <u>electrolytes</u>

* <u>CPK</u>: to assess for <u>rhabdomyolysis</u>





### Treatment [[2]](/library/gMWFLN0)[[3]](/library/B5WzmN0)[[8]](/library/x5WEmN0)




* Discontinue exercise.

* Initiate <u>passive cooling</u>

* Treat <u>dehydration</u>, typically with <u>oral rehydration therapy</u>.

* Severe <u>heat exhaustion</u>

* Consider <u>IV fluid resuscitation</u>.

* Initiate <u>evaporative and convective cooling</u>.

* Begin <u>conductive cooling</u> if refractory, i.e., manage as <u>heatstroke</u>.





> [!WARNING]
> If <u>heatstroke</u> cannot be excluded clinically, begin intensive <u>active cooling</u> without delay. [[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




### Disposition [[4]](/library/kIYm1q)[[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* Discharge after rehydration: Consider for young, healthy patients without major laboratory abnormalities.

* Hospital admission: Consider for patients with coexisting disease, advanced age, and/or significant laboratory abnormalities.

---

## Heatstroke

### Definition [[2]](/library/gMWFLN0)[[3]](/library/B5WzmN0)[[7]](/library/AeXRYx)




<u>Heatstroke</u> is a life-threatening heat-related illness characterized by all of the following:




* Significantly elevated core body temperature; typically defined as > 40.0Â°C (> 104Â°F)

* Severe <u>CNS</u> dysfunction, e.g., <u>encephalopathy</u>, <u>seizures</u>, <u>coma</u>

* Recent intense physical exertion and/or exposure to extreme heat





### Classification




| <br>Classification of heatstroke [[2]](/library/gMWFLN0)[[3]](/library/B5WzmN0)[[7]](/library/AeXRYx)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Nonexertional heatstroke (<u>classic heatstroke</u>) | Exertional heatstroke |
| Definition | <br>* <u>Heatstroke</u> primarily caused by passive exposure to high ambient temperatures<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Heatstroke</u> primarily caused by strenuous physical activity increasing heat generation<br><br>* High ambient temperatures can be a contributing factor.<br><br><br> |
| <u>Epidemiology</u> | <br>* Children, older adults, and chronically ill individuals are at high risk.<br><br> | <br>* Healthy <u>adolescents</u> and adults with occupations that involve heavy exertion are at elevated risk:<br><br>* Athletes<br><br>* Laborers, e.g., agricultural workers<br><br>* Military personnel and firefighters<br><br> |
| <u>Risk factors</u> | <br><br>* Physical disability, immobility, or confinement, e.g., institutionalized individuals, <u>infants</u><br><br>* Medical conditions that impair <u>thermoregulation</u>, e.g., cardiovascular disease, <u>obesity</u>, <u>diabetes mellitus</u>, <u>dementia</u>, <u>anhidrosis</u><br><br>* <u>Medications that impair thermoregulation</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Strenuous physical activity and/or poor physical fitness<br><br>* Environmental factors that impede heat dissipation, e.g., heavy clothing, high ambient temperatures, high <u>humidity</u><br><br>* Viral or bacterial infection<br><br>* <u>Recreational drug</u> use, e.g., <u>alcohol</u>, stimulants<br><br><br> |
| Distinct clinical features | <br>* <u>Skin</u> is usually dry.<br><br> | <br>* <u>Skin</u> is often wet, and sweating can be profuse.<br><br> |





### Clinical features [[1]](/library/SMWyLN0)[[2]](/library/gMWFLN0)[[7]](/library/AeXRYx)




* Body temperature usually > 40.0Â°C (> 104Â°F)

* Severe <u>CNS</u> dysfunction

* Persistently <u>altered mental status</u> (<u>AMS</u>)

* <u>Delirium</u>, <u>hallucinations</u>

* <u>Loss of consciousness</u>, <u>coma</u>

* <u>Seizures</u>

* <u>Ataxia</u> and <u>tremors</u>

* Hot <u>skin</u> (wet or dry)

* Flaccid or persistently rigid muscles

* <u>Tachypnea</u>

* <u>Tachycardia</u>

* <u>Hypotension</u>

* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>





### Differential diagnosis [[2]](/library/gMWFLN0)[[3]](/library/B5WzmN0)




* Causes of <u>fever</u>: e.g., infection/<u>sepsis</u>

* Other <u>causes of hyperthermia</u>, e.g., <u>stimulant intoxication</u>

* <u>Ischemic stroke</u>

* <u>High-altitude cerebral edema</u>

* <u>Electrolyte</u> abnormality

* <u>Hypoglycemia</u>

* <u>Exercise-associated hyponatremia</u>

* <u>Hypernatremia</u>





> [!WARNING]
> If there is diagnostic uncertainty about <u>heat exhaustion</u> vs. <u>heatstroke</u>, immediately begin empiric treatment for <u>heatstroke</u>.




### Diagnostics [[1]](/library/SMWyLN0)[[3]](/library/B5WzmN0)[[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




<u>Heatstroke</u> is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u>. Diagnostic studies can support the diagnosis, help rule out alternative causes, and assess for complications (e.g., <u>AKI</u>).




#### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[4]](/library/kIYm1q)[[9]](/library/SsWy850)




* <u>CBC</u>

* ↑ <u>WBC</u> (<u>stress</u> <u>leukocytosis</u>)

* ↓ <u>Platelet count</u> if there is <u>DIC</u>

* <u>CMP</u>

* Findings of <u>AKI</u> (↑ <u>BUN</u>, ↑ <u>creatinine</u>) in up to 30% of patients [[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[10]](/library/ZUXZbx)

* <u>Hypernatremia</u> or <u>hyponatremia</u>

* <u>Hyperkalemia</u> or <u>hypokalemia</u>

* <u>Hypoglycemia</u>

* ↑ <u>Transaminases</u> in hepatic injury

* <u>ABG</u>

* ↓ <u>PaO<sub>2</sub></u>

* <u>Metabolic acidosis</u> or <u>respiratory alkalosis</u>

* ↑ <u>Lactate</u>

* <u>CPK</u>, <u>myoglobin</u>: to assess for <u>rhabdomyolysis</u>

* <u>Coagulation panel</u>: to assess for <u>DIC</u>

* <u>Troponin</u>: to assess for <u>cardiomyopathy</u>





#### Additional diagnostics




* <u>ECG</u>: Nonspecific <u>ST segment abnormalities</u> and <u>ischemic ECG changes</u> may indicate <u>stress-induced cardiomyopathy</u>. [[11]](/library/Blcz_c0)

* <u>CXR</u>: Consider in patients with signs or <u>symptoms of respiratory distress</u>.

* Other <u>diagnostics for AMS</u>: e.g., CT head





### Management [[1]](/library/SMWyLN0)[[2]](/library/gMWFLN0)[[3]](/library/B5WzmN0)




#### Initial management




* Begin <u>advanced cardiac life support</u> if indicated, and perform an <u>ABCDE survey</u>.

* Initiate rapid <u>active cooling</u>. [[1]](/library/SMWyLN0)[[2]](/library/gMWFLN0)

* Goal: core body temperature < 39Â°C (< 102.2Â°F) within 30 minutes

* <u>Conductive cooling</u> with immersion in ice water is the preferred method in <u>exertional heatstroke</u>.

* <u>Evaporative and convective cooling</u> may be considered in <u>nonexertional heatstroke</u>, but the cooling rate is slower.  [[2]](/library/gMWFLN0)

* Start other <u>active cooling</u> methods immediately if immersion is not readily available.

* Begin <u>IV fluid resuscitation</u> while avoiding overhydration.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Active cooling</u> is the highest priority for patients with <u>heatstroke</u> and should be considered even before initiating transport. [[12]](/library/ysWdx50)




#### <u>Supportive care</u> and monitoring




* Initiate continuous temperature monitoring.

* <u>Replete electrolytes</u> guided by serial <u>laboratory studies</u>.

* Consider <u>benzodiazepines</u> for shivering and <u>seizures</u> [[3]](/library/B5WzmN0)[[4]](/library/kIYm1q)[[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* Monitor for and treat delayed complications (e.g., <u>management of rhabdomyolysis</u>).

* Continue cooling until:

* Normal body temperature

* Clinically stable with normal <u>CNS</u> function





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Antipyretics</u> interrupt the change in the <u>hypothalamic</u> set point caused by pyrogens and are ineffective in <u>heatstroke</u>. They may even be harmful because of the risk of bleeding. [[2]](/library/gMWFLN0)[[7]](/library/AeXRYx)




#### Disposition [[4]](/library/kIYm1q)[[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[8]](/library/x5WEmN0)




* All patients require hospital admission.

* Most patients require <u>ICU</u> admission to monitor for and manage organ failure.





### Complications [[7]](/library/AeXRYx)




* <u>Multisystem organ failure</u>

* <u>Acute respiratory distress syndrome</u>

* <u>Rhabdomyolysis</u> and <u>acute kidney injury</u>

* Acute hepatic dysfunction

* <u>Disseminated intravascular coagulation</u>

---

## Prevention

* Ensure adequate hydration and take breaks from the heat.

* Minimize the use of substances and <u>medications that impair thermoregulation</u>.

* Identify and prepare vulnerable individuals for heat events.

* Athletes: Consider heat <u>acclimatization</u>.

---
